(p-235) His Majestic and Exalted saying:

﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles around their necks, and they reach to the chins, so they are held with their heads raised.﴾ ﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and We have covered them, so they do not see.﴾

Makki said: "It is literal regarding the conditions of the Hereafter when they enter the Fire. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿'So We covered them'﴾ weakens this view, because the sight of the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection is sharp; he sees the ugliness of his state." Al-Dahhak said: its meaning is: We prevented them from spending in the way of Allah, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 29]. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Ishaq said: it is a metaphor for the state of the disbelievers who intended harm against Muhammad ﷺ, so Allah, Exalted is He, made this an example for them of the restraint of their harm toward him when they plotted against him. 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed when Abu Jahl intended to strike him with a great stone, but Allah prevented him from it, and also on other occasions. A group said: the verse is metaphorical in meaning, from Allah, Exalted is He, preventing them and placing a barrier between them and Him. This is the most preponderant of the opinions, because when He mentioned that they do not believe in what was previously decreed for them from eternity, He followed that with making for them, from the prevention and the encompassing of wretchedness, a state in which their condition is that of the vanquished.

"Al-ghull" is what encircles the neck, in the sense of constriction, fastening, punishment and restraint; together with the neck are the two hands, or one hand. This is the meaning of shackling (taghlil). His saying "fa-hiya" (so they) may refer back to the shackles, meaning: they are wide, reaching with their rims to the chins. The dhaqn is the junction of the two jaws, so the shackled one is forced to raise his face toward the sky, and that is al-iqmah (raising the head), which is akin to the posture of one made to drink or to swallow; similar to what a person and an animal do when drinking cold water, or when encountering very strong saltiness or sourness, and the like. It may also refer back to the hands, which is the view of al-Tabari, even though no mention of them has preceded, because their place in the meaning is clear, since the shackle is only in the neck together with the hands. It is narrated in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy: [Indeed We have placed in their right hands], and in some readings [in their hands]. We have already mentioned the meaning of al-iqmah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 10–12:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a generous reward.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces, and We have enumerated everything in a clear record (imam mubin).﴾

This is an address to Muhammad, upon him be peace, and its implication is consolation for him regarding them, meaning: they have been decreed to disbelief, so your warning and your not warning them are the same. The alif in His words, ﴿a'anzartahum (أأنْذَرْتَهُمْ)﴾, is the alif of equality (alif al-taswiyah), because it is not an interrogative; rather, the one who asks and the one who is asked are equal in knowledge of that.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read "a'anzartahum" with the madd (prolongation). Ibn Muhaysin and al-Zuhri read "anzartahum" with a single hamzah, as a statement (khabar). "Sawa'un" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'). His words, ﴿am lam tundhirhum (أمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهم)﴾ together with what precedes it, form a sentence of two verbs in balance, which are construed as one verb that is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. It is as if he said: "All of your action is the same to them," and this "all" is explained by "whether you warned them or did not warn them." A similar example is your saying: "It is the same to me whether you stood or sat." Abu 'Ali stated this in his clarification of the predicate, and the predicate is the subject.

His words, ﴿Innama tundhiru (إنَّما تُنْذِرُ)﴾, are not restrictive by means of "innama"; rather, they specify those whom warning benefits.

"Ittiba' al-dhikr (اتِّباعُ الذِكْرِ)" is acting upon what is in the Book of Allah, blessed and exalted, and following it. Qatadah said: "The Reminder is the Qur'an."

His words, ﴿bil-ghayb (بِالغَيْبِ)﴾, mean in private, in seclusion, when a person is hidden from the eyes of people.

Then He said, ﴿fa-bashshirhu (فَبَشِّرْهُ)﴾, using the singular pronoun in consideration of the wording of "man" (مَنِ).

"Al-ajr al-karim (الأجْرُ الكَرِيمُ)" is everything that a hired worker receives, accompanied by praise for the excellence and honour (of the work); and likewise is Paradise for the believers.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed of His giving life to the dead, in response to the disbelievers, and then threatened them by mentioning His recording of traces and His enumeration of everything. Everything a person does is included in what he has sent forward, and it also enters into his traces; however, He, blessed and exalted, mentioned the matter from both aspects, and to draw attention to the traces that remain and are mentioned after a person, whether good or bad. Otherwise, all of that is included in what the son of Adam has sent forward. Qatadah said: "What they have sent forward" means: from deeds. Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said the same. A person's example may remain, so that others follow it after him, and he is rewarded or sinful for it. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infitar: 5]. A group read "wa-athTharahum (وَآثارَهُمْ)" with the accusative, and Masruq read it with the nominative.

Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: this verse was revealed concerning the Banu Salamah when they wanted to move closer to the mosque. We have explained this at the beginning of the surah. Thabit al-Bunani said: "I walked with Anas ibn Malik to the prayer, and I hastened, and he restrained me. When the prayer was over, he said to me: 'I walked with the Prophet (ﷺ) to the prayer, and I hastened, and he restrained me. When the prayer was over, he said: "Do you not know that traces are recorded?"'" This is an argument from the verse. Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Hasan said: the "traces" in this verse are the steps. Al-Tha'labi related from Anas that he said: the steps to Friday prayer.

His words, ﴿wa-kulla (وَكُلَّ)﴾, are in the accusative governed by a hidden verb indicated by ﴿ahsaynahu (أحْصَيْناهُ)﴾; it is as if he said: "And We enumerated everything We have enumerated." "Al-imam" is the Book to which one is guided and which is a proof; Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said it means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). A group said it means the scrolls of deeds.

(p-239) His Majestic and Exalted words:

﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it.﴾ ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them both, so We strengthened them with a third, and they said, "Indeed, we are messengers to you."﴾ ﴿They said, "You are not but human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you.﴾ ﴿And upon us is only the clear notification."﴾

Ḍarb al-mathal (striking a parable) is derived from ḍarb, meaning a likeness in kind, as you say: "This struck that," meaning it resembles it. It has been disputed whether the verb ḍaraba in the phrase ḍarb al-mathal takes two objects or one. Whoever says it takes two objects makes this verse "mathalan" and "aṣḥāba" the two objects of "iḍrib" (present). Whoever says it takes one object makes it "mathalan," and makes "aṣḥāba" a substitute (badal) for it. It is also permissible for the object to be "aṣḥāba," with his saying "mathalan" in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning: in a state of representation from you.

As for "al-qarya" (the town), according to what has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-Zuhrī, it is Antioch (Anṭākiya). Regarding the messengers, Qatāda and others said: they were among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) whom ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, sent when he was raised and the one upon whom his likeness was cast was crucified, so the disciples dispersed throughout the horizons, and Allah related here the story of those who set out for Antioch. Another group said: these were prophets sent by Allah, blessed and exalted is He. This is supported by the statement of the disbelievers: "You are not but human beings like us," for this is a dialogue that is only said to one who conveys a message from Allah, whereas the other view is merely possible. Al-Naqqāsh mentioned in the narratives of this verse things that are lengthy, and their authenticity is not certain, so I have abridged them.

What is necessarily implied by the verse is that Allah sent to it two messengers, and they called the people of the town to worship Allah alone and to guidance and faith, but they denied them. So Allah, exalted is He, strengthened their mission with a third, and the proof was established against the people of the town. A man from among them who came running believed, but they killed him at the end of his affair and disbelieved, so a blast from the sky struck them and they were extinguished.

The majority of reciters read ﴿"fa-ʿazzaznā"﴾ with the first zāy doubled, meaning: We strengthened and reinforced, and Mujāhid and others explained it this way. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of al-Mufaḍḍal from Abū Bakr, read it with the zāy lightened, meaning: We overcame their affair. In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd it is "bi-al-thālith" with an alif and lām.

(p-239) His Majestic and Exalted words:

﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it.﴾ ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them both, so We strengthened them with a third, and they said, "Indeed, we are messengers to you."﴾ ﴿They said, "You are not but human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you.﴾ ﴿And upon us is only the clear notification."﴾

Ḍarb al-mathal (striking a parable) is derived from ḍarb, meaning a likeness in kind, as you say: "This struck that," meaning it resembles it. It has been disputed whether the verb ḍaraba in the phrase ḍarb al-mathal takes two objects or one. Whoever says it takes two objects makes this verse "mathalan" and "aṣḥāba" the two objects of "iḍrib" (present). Whoever says it takes one object makes it "mathalan," and makes "aṣḥāba" a substitute (badal) for it. It is also permissible for the object to be "aṣḥāba," with his saying "mathalan" in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning: in a state of representation from you.

As for "al-qarya" (the town), according to what has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-Zuhrī, it is Antioch (Anṭākiya). Regarding the messengers, Qatāda and others said: they were among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) whom ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, sent when he was raised and the one upon whom his likeness was cast was crucified, so the disciples dispersed throughout the horizons, and Allah related here the story of those who set out for Antioch. Another group said: these were prophets sent by Allah, blessed and exalted is He. This is supported by the statement of the disbelievers: "You are not but human beings like us," for this is a dialogue that is only said to one who conveys a message from Allah, whereas the other view is merely possible. Al-Naqqāsh mentioned in the narratives of this verse things that are lengthy, and their authenticity is not certain, so I have abridged them.

What is necessarily implied by the verse is that Allah sent to it two messengers, and they called the people of the town to worship Allah alone and to guidance and faith, but they denied them. So Allah, exalted is He, strengthened their mission with a third, and the proof was established against the people of the town. A man from among them who came running believed, but they killed him at the end of his affair and disbelieved, so a blast from the sky struck them and they were extinguished.

The majority of reciters read ﴿"fa-ʿazzaznā"﴾ with the first zāy doubled, meaning: We strengthened and reinforced, and Mujāhid and others explained it this way. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of al-Mufaḍḍal from Abū Bakr, read it with the zāy lightened, meaning: We overcame their affair. In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd it is "bi-al-thālith" with an alif and lām.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 18–21:

The Exalted's words:

﴿They said, "We take omens from you. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment will surely touch you from us."﴾ ﴿They said, "Your omen is with you. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a people who transgress."﴾ ﴿And from the farthest part of the city came a man, running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers.﴾ ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and who are guided."﴾

Some of the interpreters said: The disease of leprosy (al-judham) spread quickly among the people of this town when they denied the messengers, and so they said, "We take omens from you." Muqatil said: The rain was withheld from them, and so they said it. Its meaning is: "We regard you as a bad omen." It is derived from judging by birds (al-hukm bil-tayr, augury), and this meaning is common among the nations. The verb tatayyartu is rarely used except for ill omen. As for the judging by birds among those who practise it, it covers both good and bad omens. The more evident view is that the augury of these people arose from the division of the word and the tempting of the people that had come upon their town. This is similar to the augury of the Quraysh regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and similar to what was addressed to Musa (peace be upon him). Qatada said: "If evil befalls us, it is only because of you." The phrase "la-narjumannakum" means: with stones. Qatada, may God be pleased with him, said this. Their words, "Your omen is with you" (ṭā'irukum ma'akum), mean: your fortune, and whatever evil or good comes to you, is with you, that is, from your own deeds and your earnings. It is not from us, nor because of us, but because of your transgression and your disbelief. The people interpreted it this way. The word ṭā'ir (bird, omen) was used figuratively for fortune and share, meaning that it is what results from observing the birds. This meaning became so common that the Ansari woman said: "The emigrant 'Uthman ibn Maz'un's ṭā'ir (lot) flew for us when the emigrants were divided." The jurists say: "The ṭā'ir flew for so-and-so in the muhassa (the division of shares) for such-and-such."

Ibn Hurmuz, al-Hasan, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read ṭayrukum (tayrukum). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿a-in﴾ with two hamzas, the second being kasra, meaning: "Is it because you were reminded that you take omens?" Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Kathir read this second hamza as softened and turned into a ya', "ayna dhukkirtum." al-Majshun read "an" with a fatha on the alif. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "in dhukkirtum" with a kasra on the alif. Abu 'Amr, in some of what is transmitted from him, and Zirr ibn Hubaysh also read "a-an" with two open hamzas. Its witness is the poet's saying:

Because you are the one with two cloaks, dark and well-combed,
you are not a guardian for your cousin's forbidden [women].

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and al-A'mash read "ayn" with the ya' sukun, and "dhukirtum" with the kaf lightened. This is then the "ayn" of place (al-zarf). This is the reading of Khalid, Talha, Qatada, and al-Hasan, who lightened only the kaf.

Then He, exalted be He, described them as wasteful and transgressing.

Exalted and blessed is His mention, He informs us about the condition of a man who came from the farthest part of the city. He had heard from the messengers and understood from God, so he came running on his feet and heard their words. When he understood them, it is related that he followed up on their affair and tested them by saying: "Do you ask for a reward for this call of yours?" They said, "No." At that point he called his people to follow them and to believe in them, since they were the truth. Then he argued against them with his words: "Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and who are guided," that is, while they are upon guidance from God. This verse establishes the deficiency of one who takes a wage for anything among the acts of the Law that are obligatory, such as prayer and the like, since it is like conveying the message for which one was sent. This differs from what is not obligatory for him, such as governorship and judgeship. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, took a stipend (irtazaqa).

It is related from Abu Mijlaz, Ka'b al-Ahbar, and Ibn 'Abbas that the name of this man was Habib, and that he was a carpenter. Wahb ibn Munabbih said he had been afflicted with leprosy. It was also said that he was in a cave worshipping his Lord. Ibn Abi Layla said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who never disbelieved in God for the blink of an eye: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him; the companion of Ya-Sin; and the believer of the family of Pharaoh." People have mentioned among the names of the messengers: Sadiq, Sadus, and Shalum, and other than these, but the authenticity is absent, so I have abridged.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verse 22–27:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And why should I not worship He who created me, and to whom you will be returned?﴾ ﴿Shall I take other gods besides Him? If the Most Merciful intends me any harm, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I would then be in clear error.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ ﴿It was said: "Enter Paradise." He said: "Would that my people knew, ﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured."﴾

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿"wa-ma liya"﴾ with a fatha on the ya', while al-A'mash and Hamza read it with a sukun on the ya'. This has been discussed before.

His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-ma liya," is a rebuke directed at them, in the form of reproach, concerning a matter which reason testifies to be sound: that He who originated, invented and brought into existence from non-existence is the One who deserves to be worshipped. Then he informed them that they would be gathered to Him on the Day of Resurrection. Then he also made them stand, in the form of reproach, before the taking of other gods besides God, which cannot avert from them the decrees that God intends for them, neither by any power of their own nor by intercession. Talha al-Samman and 'Isa al-Hamdani read ﴿"yaruddni"﴾ with an open ya' (p-243), and it is narrated from 'Asim, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr.

Then he openly declared his faith and proclaimed it, saying: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ The exegetes differed. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, Ka'b and Wahb said: he addressed his people with it in the form of emphasis and admonition. It was also said: he addressed the messengers with it, in the form of calling them as witnesses and asking them to preserve the matter with them. The majority read the nun with a kasra, intending a ya' after it, while Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim its fatha. Abu Hatim said: this is an error and is not permissible, because it is a command; so either the nun is dropped or it is kasra in intention of the ya'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Here there is an omitted matter, which the narrations and reports have transmitted with certainty: that they killed him. It is disputed how. Qatada and others said: they stoned him with stones. Ibn Mas'ud said: they walked over him with their feet until his intestines came out from his rear. It was said to him at his death: ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ That was, Allah knows best, by his being shown his station in it, and his being certain that he was among its inhabitants through seeing what gladdened his eye. When he attained that, he wished that his people would know of it. It was said: he intended by that compassion and sincere advice for them, i.e., if they knew of it they would believe in Allah. It was also said: he intended that they would regret their action against him and be grieved by it. This exists in human nature: when a person attains good in a land of estrangement, he wishes that his neighbours and peers among whom he grew up would know of it, especially regarding honours. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"Honour is sought and pursued, / and most beloved is what is attained in one's homeland."

The first interpretation is more fitting for this righteous servant, and concerning that the Prophet ﷺ said: "He advised his people while living and dead." Qatada ibn Di'ama said: he advised them in a state of anger and of contentment, and likewise the believer, you will find him only sincerely advising people.

The "ma" in His saying, ﴿bima ghafara﴾, may be a verbal (masdariyya) particle, i.e., "by the forgiveness of my Lord to me," and it may be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), and in "ghafara" there is a returning pronoun. Al-Zuhri said: it may also be interrogative, then he weakened this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 28–32:

The Exalted said:

﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever to send down.﴾ ﴿It was but one Cry, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾ ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they will not return to them?﴾ ﴿And all of them, every one, will be brought before Us.﴾

This is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ) in which there is a threat to Quraysh, for this is what frightens them as an example: that there should descend upon them from the punishment of Allah what descended upon the people of Habib al-Najjar. So He (glorified and exalted be He) negated, meaning: He did not send down upon the people of this man any host from the heaven. Mujahid said: He meant that He did not send a messenger to them, nor did He seek to make them repent. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: He meant that He did not need, in punishing them, any of the hosts of Allah, such as stones, drowning, wind, and other things; rather it was one single Cry, because they were easier and lower than that. Qatada said: By Allah, Allah did not admonish His people after killing him until He destroyed them.

The commentators differed concerning His saying: ﴿nor were We ever to send down﴾. One group said: "ma" is negating, and this goes with the second interpretation of His saying: ﴿We did not send down upon his people after him any host﴾. Another group said: "ma" is coordinated with "jund" (host), meaning: "any host, and that which We were sending down upon nations like them before that."

The majority read "illa sayhatan" (إلّا صَيْحَةً) with a fatha, as the predicate of "kana" (كانَ), meaning: their punishment was not but one single Cry. Abu Ja'far and Mu'adh ibn al-Harith read "illa sayhatun wahidatun" (إلّا صَيْحَةٌ واحِدَةٌ) with a damma. Abu Hatim considered this weak, and its correct reading is that it is not the "kana" that requires a subject and predicate; rather the sense is: "there occurred or happened nothing but one single Cry." Ibn Mas'ud and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad read "illa zaqyatan wahidatan" (إلّا زَقْيَةً واحِدَةً), and zaqya is the cry of a rooster or similar birds.

"Khamidun" (خامِدُونَ): silent, dead, lying prostrate on the ground; they were likened to ashes whose fire has gone out and been extinguished.

His saying: ﴿"Alas"﴾ (يا حَسْرَةً) is a vocative addressed to it, meaning: this is the time of your presence and manifestation. This is the estimate of such a vocative according to Sibawayh, and it is a sound meaning in itself; and it is an indefinite vocative in this reading. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: "Alas, the regret of the servants over themselves," and he mentioned that it is so in some readings. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: the meaning is: "Woe to the servants." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Ali ibn al-Husayn, Mujahid, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "Alas for the servants" (يا حَسْرَةَ العِبادِ) with the idafa. The saying of Ibn 'Abbas is good in light of this reading, while al-Tabari's interpretation of the first reading is not clear; rather, it is more fitting that the meaning is a lament over the servants, as the situation requires, and the nature of every human being requires, upon hearing their state and their punishment for disbelief and their neglect of the command of Allah the Exalted, that one feel pity and grieve for the servants. Abu al-'Aliya said: what is meant by "the servants" is the three messengers, so this grief would be from the disbelievers, who, when they saw the punishment of Allah, lamented what had escaped them. His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾ and so on, refutes this interpretation.

"Hasra" (الحَسْرَةُ) is the laments that leave their owner exhausted. Al-A'raj, Muslim ibn Jundub, and Abu al-Zinad read "ya hasrah" (يا حَسْرَهْ) with a pause on the ha', in order to emphasize the meaning of grief and to establish it in the soul; pronouncing the ha' in such a case is more eloquent in causing sorrow and stirring the soul, like their saying: "awwih" and the like. His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾ and so on, is an illustration of the deed of Quraysh.

Then He meant them by His saying: ﴿Have they not seen how many﴾; "kam" here is khabariyya (declarative), "annahum" is a substitute for it, and "al-ru'ya" is sight of the eye. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Have they not seen whom We destroyed?" The majority read "annahum" with a fatha on the alif, and al-Hasan al-Basri read it with a kasra. The majority read "lamma" with a light mim, the "ma" being added for emphasis, and the meaning is "all of them"; al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and 'Asim doubled the mim, saying: it is placed in the position of "illa" (except); and it was said: the intended reading is "lamimma," one of them having been elided, though this is weak. In the reading of Ubayy: [And there is not among them any but that a gathering of them will be brought before Us]. Qatada said: they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 33–36:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have revived it and brought forth from it grain, and from it they eat.﴾ ﴿And We placed in it gardens of palm trees and grapes, and We caused springs to gush forth within it.﴾ ﴿That they may eat of its fruit, and that which their hands have made. Will they not then be grateful?﴾ ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of that which they do not know.﴾

"Ayah" (sign) means: a proof of the Gathering (hashr) and the resurrection of bodies. The pronoun in "lahum" (for them) is intended to refer to the disbelievers of Quraysh. Nafi', Shayba and Abu Ja'far read "al-maytah" with a kasra on the ya' and its shadda, while Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read it with a sukun on the ya' and without shadda (lightened). Its reviving is by means of rain.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "thamarihi" with a fatha on the tha' and the mim. Talha, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read both with a damma. Al-A'mash read it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. As for the pronoun in it: one group said it refers to the water implied by His saying, "from the springs" (min al-'uyun), since the sense is: "ma" [i.e., the water]. Another group said it refers to everything mentioned previously in summary, as if He had said: "from the fruit of what We have mentioned." Abu 'Ubayda said it is of the type where a person mentions two or three things and then returns the pronoun to one of them and refers to it by a pronoun, as al-Azraq ibn Tarafa ibn al-'Amarrad al-Firasi al-Bahili said:

"He threw me with a sin, of which I and my father were innocent, and because of the well he threw me."

This interpretation of the verse is weak.

As for "ma" in His saying, "and that which their hands have made": al-Tabari said it is a noun conjoined to "the fruit," meaning: eating occurs from the fruit and from what hands have made by planting, cultivation and the like. Another group said it is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and it was said it is a negative particle, the sense being: they eat from its fruit, and it is something their hands did not make, rather it is a blessing from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, upon them. The majority of reciters read "'amilat-hu" with the pronoun ha'; Hamza, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, Talha and 'Isa read "'amilat" without a pronoun.

Then, Blessed and Exalted is He, declared Himself free of all imperfection absolutely, from everything that the heretic deviates into or that the polytheist associates. "Al-azwaj" (the pairs) means: the kinds of every thing. His saying, "and of that which they do not know," is similar to His saying: "and He creates what you do not know" (al-Nahl: 8).

"Ayah" (sign) means: a proof of the Gathering (hashr) and the resurrection of bodies. The pronoun in "lahum" (for them) is intended to refer to the disbelievers of Quraysh. Nafi', Shayba and Abu Ja'far read "al-maytah" with a kasra on the ya' and its shadda, while Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read it with a sukun on the ya' and without shadda (lightened). Its reviving is by means of rain.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "thamarihi" with a fatha on the tha' and the mim. Talha, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read both with a damma. Al-A'mash read it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. As for the pronoun in it: one group said it refers to the water implied by His saying, "from the springs" (min al-'uyun), since the sense is: "ma" [i.e., the water]. Another group said it refers to everything mentioned previously in summary, as if He had said: "from the fruit of what We have mentioned." Abu 'Ubayda said it is of the type where a person mentions two or three things and then returns the pronoun to one of them and refers to it by a pronoun, as al-Azraq ibn Tarafa ibn al-'Amarrad al-Firasi al-Bahili said:

"He threw me with a sin, of which I and my father were innocent, and because of the well he threw me."

This interpretation of the verse is weak.

As for "ma" in His saying, "and that which their hands have made": al-Tabari said it is a noun conjoined to "the fruit," meaning: eating occurs from the fruit and from what hands have made by planting, cultivation and the like. Another group said it is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and it was said it is a negative particle, the sense being: they eat from its fruit, and it is something their hands did not make, rather it is a blessing from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, upon them. The majority of reciters read "'amilat-hu" with the pronoun ha'; Hamza, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, Talha and 'Isa read "'amilat" without a pronoun.

Then, Blessed and Exalted is He, declared Himself free of all imperfection absolutely, from everything that the heretic deviates into or that the polytheist associates. "Al-azwaj" (the pairs) means: the kinds of every thing. His saying, "and of that which they do not know," is similar to His saying: "and He creates what you do not know" (al-Nahl: 8).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verse 37–40:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ ﴿And the sun runs on to a fixed course for it. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And the moon—We have measured for it stations, until it returns like the old withered stalk of a palm-branch.﴾ ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each is floating in an orbit.﴾

These verses are what God, exalted is He, made as evidence of His power and of the necessity of His being the sole God. "NasKhalu" (نَسْلَخُ) means: We peel off and strip away; it is thus a metaphor. "Muzlimun" (مُظْلِمُونَ) means: entering into darkness. Some people have derived from this verse that the night is the original and the day is a later addition upon it, but there is room for scrutiny in this.

As for "the sun's fixed course" (مُسْتَقَرُّ الشَمْسِ), according to what has been related in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him): "Beneath the Throne, where she prostrates every night after her setting." And in another hadith: "that she prostrates in a murky spring, and there is a great fall for her there." A group said: its fixed course is on the Day of Resurrection, when it is folded up, so it runs toward that fixed course. Another group said: its fixed course is a metaphor for its disappearances, since it runs at every time toward a bounded limit in which it sets. It was also said: its fixed course is its furthest rising points in the two turnings (al-munqalabayn), because they are the endpoints of its risings; when it reaches them it turns back, and otherwise it does not rest from its motion even for the blink of an eye. Ibn Qutayba inclined to this view. Another group said: its fixed course is its standing still at midday (al-zawal) each day, and the evidence of its standing still is that the shadows of things stand still at that time.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them) read: "لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها" (there is no fixed course for it).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj read "والقَمَرُ" with a nominative ending, coordinated with "اللَيْلُ" (the night), a coordination of one clause with another. Another possibility is also valid: that "وآيَةٌ لَهُمُ" (and a sign for them) be a beginning (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, as if he said: in existence and in observation. Then he explained that with two clauses of beginning and predicate: the night is the first, and the moon is the second. The rest read "القَمَرَ" (in the accusative) by supposing a verb implied, which is explained by "قَدَّرْناهُ" (We have measured it). This is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin, and al-Hasan, according to one of the transmissions from him.

"Manazil" (مَنازِلَ) is in the accusative as an adverb of place/time. These are the well-known stations among the Arabs, twenty-eight stations, through which the moon passes each night, less than one of them, as they claim. Its return (عَوْدَتُهُ) is its beginning to appear thin, and then it resembles the 'urjun (العُرْجُونِ), which is the branch of the palm tree bearing the clusters of dates; when it grows old, it bends and turns yellow, and it becomes most like the crescent. This was said by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, and existence bears witness to it. Sulayman al-Taymi read "كالعِرْجُونِ" with a kasra on the ayn. "Al-qadim" (القَدِيمِ) means: the old one over which a long time has passed.

"Yanbaghi" (يَنْبَغِي) is used here for what cannot be opposed, because they have no power to do otherwise. The majority read "سابِقُ النَهارِ" with the genitive construction. 'Ubada read "سابِقُ النَهارَ" without tanwin on the qaf and with the accusative on "النَهارَ"; al-Zahrawi mentioned it and said: he dropped the tanwin for lightness. "Al-falak" (الفَلَكُ), according to what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), is a moving, round thing like the whorl of a spindle, in which all the stars are. "Yasbahun" (يَسْبَحُونَ) means: they run and swim. Makki said: when the verb of one who has intellect was attributed to them, they were pluralized with the waw and nun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 41–46:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ ﴿and created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾ ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry out for them, nor are they rescued﴾ ﴿except as a mercy from Us and as enjoyment for a time﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you, that perhaps you may be shown mercy"﴾ ﴿And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them except that they turn away from it﴾

"Āyah" (sign) means a sign and an indication. Its nominative case is due to it being the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is in His saying, "for them" (lahum). "Annā" (that We) is a substitute (badal) for "āyah", though this is open to question. It is also possible that "an" is explanatory (mufassirah) and has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). "Al-ḥaml" (carrying) is preventing a thing from falling downward. He mentioned "offspring" (dhurriyyah) because of their weakness in travel, so the blessing among them is more apparent.

Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir and al-A'mash read "dhurriyyātihim" in the plural, and the rest read it in the singular, which is also the reading of Ṭalḥah and 'Īsā. The pronoun attached to "dhurriyyāt" is the pronoun of the genus, as if he said: "the offspring of their kind or type." This is the most correct interpretation of this point. Some people confused this matter, to the extent that they said: "dhurriyyah" applies to the forefathers, and this is not known in the Arabic language.

As for the meaning of the verse, it admits of two interpretations. The first, said by Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) and a group, is that by "the offspring" (dhurriyyāt) he means those carried, the companions of Noah (peace be upon him) in the ark, and by His saying, "of its likeness" he means the ships existing among the children of Adam until the Day of Resurrection, and it is these that He intended by His saying, "And if We will, We drown them." The second interpretation, said by Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and also related from Ibn 'Abbās, is that by His saying, "that We carried their offspring" (the verse) he means the ships existing among the children of Adam until the Day of Resurrection, and by His saying, "and created for them" (the verse) he means camels and all else that is ridden. The likeness then lies in the fact that each is a mount conveying to the regions only, and His saying, "And if We will, We drown them," refers to the ships existing among people. As for one who mixed the two views, making the offspring in the ark refer to the people of Noah in his ship, and making "of its likeness" refer to camels, this is a corrupt reasoning, which His saying, "And if We will, We drown them," refutes, so reflect upon it.

"Al-fulk" is a collective noun, and its singular is in its pattern, but the vowels of the plural are not the vowels of the singular. "Al-mashḥūn" means laden, loaded. "Min" in His saying, "of its likeness," may, according to one of the two interpretations, be partitive, and according to the other, be explanatory of the genus, so consider it. It is said: camels are the vehicles of the land.

"Al-ṣarīkh" here is in the form of the active participle, in the sense of "al-muṣrikh" (one who responds to a cry for help). That is because you say "ṣārikh" meaning one who seeks help, and "muṣrikh" meaning one who grants help, and "ṣarīkh" comes once with this meaning and once with that meaning, since "faʿīl" is among the patterns of the active participle. So at times it comes from "ṣarakha" when he sought help, and at times it comes from "aṣrakha" when he granted help.

As for His saying, "except as a mercy," al-Kisā'ī said: it is accusative as an exception, as if he said: "except that We have mercy on them." al-Zajjāj said: he put "raḥmatan" in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlih), as if he said: "except for the sake of Our mercy towards them." As for His saying, "matā'an" (enjoyment), it is conjoined to His saying, "raḥmatan" (mercy), and "ilā ḥīn" (for a time) means until their appointed terms.

The sentence is complete at His saying, "And if We will, We drown them." His saying, "there is no one to cry out for them" is a resumed statement about those who travel the sea, whether they are saved or drowned; for them, in this condition, there is no salvation except by the mercy of Allah. His saying, "there is no one to cry out for them," is not tied to the drowned, though it is possible to connect it to them, but the first is better, so reflect.

Then he began to inform about the arrogance of the Quraysh with His saying, "And when it is said to them" (the verse). "What is before them" – Muqātil and Qatādah said: it is the punishment of the nations who preceded them in time, and "what is behind them" is the punishment of the Hereafter which comes after them in time, and this is the view. al-Ḥasan said: they were warned of what had passed of their sins and what would come of them, and this is similar in meaning to the first, because fear of sin is only fear of its punishment and the recompense for it. "What is before them" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind them" is the punishment of the nations.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

"Al-ṣarīkh" here is in the form of the active participle, in the sense of "al-muṣrikh" (one who responds to a cry for help). That is because you say "ṣārikh" meaning one who seeks help, and "muṣrikh" meaning one who grants help, and "ṣarīkh" comes once with this meaning and once with that meaning, since "faʿīl" is among the patterns of the active participle. So at times it comes from "ṣarakha" when he sought help, and at times it comes from "aṣrakha" when he granted help.

As for His saying, "except as a mercy," al-Kisā'ī said: it is accusative as an exception, as if he said: "except that We have mercy on them." al-Zajjāj said: he put "raḥmatan" in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlih), as if he said: "except for the sake of Our mercy towards them." As for His saying, "matā'an" (enjoyment), it is conjoined to His saying, "raḥmatan" (mercy), and "ilā ḥīn" (for a time) means until their appointed terms.

The sentence is complete at His saying, "And if We will, We drown them." His saying, "there is no one to cry out for them" is a resumed statement about those who travel the sea, whether they are saved or drowned; for them, in this condition, there is no salvation except by the mercy of Allah. His saying, "there is no one to cry out for them," is not tied to the drowned, though it is possible to connect it to them, but the first is better, so reflect.

Then he began to inform about the arrogance of the Quraysh with His saying, "And when it is said to them" (the verse). "What is before them" – Muqātil and Qatādah said: it is the punishment of the nations who preceded them in time, and "what is behind them" is the punishment of the Hereafter which comes after them in time, and this is the view. al-Ḥasan said: they were warned of what had passed of their sins and what would come of them, and this is similar in meaning to the first, because fear of sin is only fear of its punishment and the recompense for it. "What is before them" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind them" is the punishment of the nations.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

He made the ordering as though they were moving from one thing to another, and did not consider the existence of things in time. This view is forced upon it by His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿confirming what is before it of the Torah﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 46]. What is consistently applied is to measure "what is before the hand" and "what is behind" by what time brings along, so reflect. The response of "idhā" (when) in this verse is omitted, its estimate being: they turned away, and His, the Glorified, saying explains it: ﴿except that they were turning away from it﴾. And "al-āyāt" (the signs) are the indications and proofs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 47–50:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed? You are only in clear error."﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿They await only a single blast which will seize them while they are disputing.﴾ ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor will they return to their people.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "lahum" (to them) refers to the Quraysh. The occasion of this verse was that when the disbelievers' close associates and dependants from among the clients and others among the weak became Muslim, the disbelievers cut off their maintenance and all their ties with them. At first, in Makkah, there was some contact at the time of the verses of truce (al-muwada'a, the verses concerning mutual non-aggression), so those believers urged their disbelieving relatives to maintain ties with them and to spend on them from what Allah had provided. At that, they said: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ Al-Rummani said: "They forgot the obligation of compassion and the bond of kinship."

Another group said: its occasion was that the Quraysh, because of a famine, became stingy toward the needy in general, whether believers or others, so the Prophet (ﷺ) urged them to spend on the needy, and they said this statement.

Their saying admits of two interpretations. One of them proceeds from the choices of the ignorant Arabs. It is related that a Bedouin used to graze his camels, and he would place the fat ones in the fertile land and the lean ones in the barren place. When he was asked about this, he said: "I honour what Allah has honoured, and I humiliate what Allah has humiliated." On this meaning, the saying of the Quraysh would be as if they saw withholding from one whom Allah has withheld His provision as correct. Among their proverbs is: "Be with Allah against the one who turns his back" (p-253).

The second interpretation is that their speech is meant as mockery of the words of Muhammad (ﷺ) that there is a god who is the Provider. It is as if they said: "Why does your god, whom you claim, not provide for them?" That is: "We do not feed the one whom this god you claim would feed if He willed." This is like a man who claims he is wealthy and then needs your help with money, so you say to him, by way of rebuke and mockery: "Do you seek my help while you are rich?" That is: according to your own claim.

His saying: ﴿You are only in clear error﴾ may be from the speech of the disbelievers to the believers, meaning: in your command to us to spend our wealth, and in other matters of your religion. It may also be from the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, to the disbelievers, in which He resumed rebuking them with this.

Then He related of them, as a way of holding them to account, their saying: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ That is: when is the Day of Resurrection of which you speak? It was also said: they meant, "When is this punishment with which you threaten us?" They called it a "promise" (wa'd) in a context where the indications of the speech show that it concerns evil; the word "wa'd," when used without qualification, refers to good, and when it is restricted by an indication of evil it is used for that; whereas "wa'id" (threat) is always used for evil.

"Yanzurun" means "yantaziruna" (they await), and "ma" is a negation particle. This blast is the blast of the Resurrection, the first blowing of the Trumpet, as related by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ). In a hadith it is stated that after it comes the blast of the swoon, then the blast of gathering, and it is the one that endures, for "there is no respite (fawaq) from it."

(p-254) Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj, Shibl, and Ibn Qusṭanṭin al-Makki read [yakhassimun] with a fatha on the yā' and the khā', and a shadda on the sād with a kasra, its original form being yakhtasimun: the vowel of the tā' was transferred to the khā', and the silent tā' was assimilated into the sād. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr also read it with a fatha on the yā', a sukun on the khā', and a shadda on the kasrah sād. In this reading two silent letters are brought together, but this is not a true gathering of two sukuns; Abu 'Ali explained it, and its original form is yakhtasimun: the vowel of the tā' was dropped without transfer, and the tā' was assimilated into the sād. 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' also, al-Hasan, and Abu 'Amr (in a differing report from him) read with a fatha on the yā', a kasra on the khā', and a shadda on the kasrah sād; its original form is yakhtasimun, which was treated as the previous one and then the khā' was given a kasra for the sake of meeting of two sukuns. A group read with a kasra on the yā' and the khā', and a shadda on the kasrah sād, like the one before it, then the khā's kasra was made to follow the yā's kasra. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "yakhtasimun." The meaning of all these readings is that they dispute with one another, argue their positions among themselves, and push back against one another regarding their affairs. Hamzah read "yakhsimun" (with a sukun on the khā'). This reading admits of two meanings: one of them is what is in the readings before it, that is, some of them dispute with others; the second is that they dispute with the people of truth according to their own claim, as if He said: the blast seizes them while they think of themselves that they have won or prevailed, because you say: "khasamtu fulanan fakhasamtuhu" (I disputed with so-and-so, and I defeated him) when you overcome him.

His saying: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ is an expression for the suddenness of the situation. "Tawsiyah" (bequest) is a verbal noun from "wassa" (to bequeath). His saying: ﴿nor will they return to their people﴾ admits of several interpretations. First: no one will return to his home and his family because of the urgency of the matter; rather, his soul will be taken wherever the blast seizes him. Second: its meaning is: nor will they return to their people in speech, and this is more emphatic in expressing urgency. He specified "their people" by mention because speaking with them at that time is more important to a person than with strangers, and more firmly fixed in human souls. Third: its estimation is: nor will they return to their people ever, and so this departs from the meaning of describing urgency to the meaning of mentioning their cutting off and severance from their worldly life.

The majority read "yarji'un" with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the jīm. Ibn Muhaysin read it with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatha on the jīm.

In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "yakhtasimun." The meaning of all these readings is that they dispute with one another, argue their positions among themselves, and push back against one another regarding their affairs. Hamzah read "yakhsimun" (with a sukun on the khā'). This reading admits of two meanings: one of them is what is in the readings before it, that is, some of them dispute with others; the second is that they dispute with the people of truth according to their own claim, as if He said: the blast seizes them while they think of themselves that they have won or prevailed, because you say: "khasamtu fulanan fakhasamtuhu" (I disputed with so-and-so, and I defeated him) when you overcome him.

His saying: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ is an expression for the suddenness of the situation. "Tawsiyah" (bequest) is a verbal noun from "wassa" (to bequeath). His saying: ﴿nor will they return to their people﴾ admits of several interpretations. First: no one will return to his home and his family because of the urgency of the matter; rather, his soul will be taken wherever the blast seizes him. Second: its meaning is: nor will they return to their people in speech, and this is more emphatic in expressing urgency. He specified "their people" by mention because speaking with them at that time is more important to a person than with strangers, and more firmly fixed in human souls. Third: its estimation is: nor will they return to their people ever, and so this departs from the meaning of describing urgency to the meaning of mentioning their cutting off and severance from their worldly life.

The majority read "yarji'un" with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the jīm. Ibn Muhaysin read it with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatha on the jīm.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 51–54:

(p-255) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And the Horn will be blown, and behold, from their graves they will hasten to their Lord.﴾ ﴿They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast, and behold, they will all be brought before Us.﴾ ﴿So on that Day no soul will be wronged in the least, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾

This is the blast of resurrection. As for "al-Sur" (the Horn), it is the trumpet according to the saying of the group of exegetes, and by this the reports have been transmitted through successive chains. Abu 'Ubayda held that it is the plural of "sura" (form), coming out in the pattern of "busr" and "busra," and likewise he said "surat al-bina'" (a course of a building) whose plural is "suwar." The meaning according to him and according to those who follow his view is: it will be blown into the forms (suwar) of the children of Adam, and they will return living. "Al-Ajdath" are the graves. Al-A'raj read "fi al-Sur" with a fatha on the waw, as the plural of "sura." "Yansiluna" means they walk with the gait of a wolf, quickly; and from it is the saying of the poet:

"A wolf's swift gait, when he drew near at evening, / the night grew cold upon him so he sped on."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Yansiluna" means they will come out. The majority read it with a kasra on the sin, while Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu 'Amr read it with a damma.

(p-256) Their cry "woe" (al-wayl) carries the meaning: this is your time and the moment of your presence. It is a vocative construction with an attached noun, and it is possible that its being in the accusative is as a verbal noun (masdar) with the vocative particle omitted, as if they said: "O our people, woe to us!" Ibn Abi Layla read "ya waylatana" with the feminine ta'. The majority read "man ba'athana" as an interrogative. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they read "min ba'thina" with a kasra on the mim of "min," a sukun on the 'ayn, and a kasra on the tha' in "ba'thina," in the accusative as a verbal noun. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "man ahabbana min marqadina," and in the reading of Ubayy: "man habbana." Abu al-Fath said: I have not found a basis for it in the language, and "mahbub" has not occurred to us; Abu Hatim attributed it to Ibn Mas'ud. Their saying "from our resting place" may mean the actual place of sleep, and it is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Qatada, and Mujahid that all of mankind will sleep one sleep before the gathering.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not sound in its chain of transmission. The correct understanding of their saying "from our resting place" is that it is a metaphor and a comparison, as you say of a slain man: "This is his resting place until the Day of Resurrection." In al-Tha'labi it is said that they said "from our resting place" because the punishment of the grave was like sleep compared with what they came to of the punishment of Hell. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that "this" refers to the resting place, and then he begins anew with the words: ﴿what the Most Merciful promised﴾, the predicate being implied as "true" or something similar. The majority held that the beginning of the speech is: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾.

It has been disputed who said this statement. Ibn Zayd said: it is from the words of the disbelievers when they saw the resurrection and rising that they used to deny in the world. A group said: it is from the words of Allah, blessed and exalted, to them by way of rebuke and reproach. Al-Farra' said: it is from the words of the angels. Qatada and Mujahid said: it is from the words of the believers to the disbelievers by way of reproach.

(p-257) Then Allah, exalted, informed that the matter of the Resurrection and of rising from the graves is nothing but a single blast, and then all of them are present and gathered. One group read "illa sayhatan" with the accusative, and another with the nominative; the grammatical analysis of its like has been discussed previously.

His saying "fa-al-yawma" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and it means the Day of Gathering mentioned; and this address may be understood as directed to the whole world.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 55–61:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joyful occupation.﴾ ﴿They and their spouses are in shade, reclining upon couches.﴾ ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for.﴾ ﴿"Peace!" – a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿"And stand apart today, O you criminals!"﴾ ﴿"Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan – indeed, he is to you a clear enemy – ﴾ ﴿"and that you should worship Me? This is a straight path."﴾

This is a report from Allah, the Exalted, about the state of the people of the Garden after His mention of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and the condition of the disbelievers.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Talha and Khalid ibn Ilyas read "fi shughl" (فِي شُغْلٍ) with a damma on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn. The rest read "fi shughul" (فِي شُغُلٍ) with a damma on both, which is the reading of the people of Madina and Kufa. Mujahid and Abu 'Amr also read it with a fatha on both. Ibn Hubayra read it from the pulpit with a fatha on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn. All of these have one meaning.

The scholars differed over the specification of this occupation. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyib said: the deflowering of virgins. al-Naqqash related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is: listening to stringed instruments. Mujahid said: its meaning is a bliss that has occupied them. This is the sound view, since specifying one thing over another has no basis. Since all bliss is one type insofar as it is bliss, He said "fi shughl" (in occupation), and had it varied He would have said "fi ashghal" (in occupations). al-Tha'labi related from Tawus that he said: "If the people of the Garden knew from whom they were occupied, what they were occupied with would not give them pleasure." al-Tha'labi said: Some scholars were asked about the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Most of the people of the Garden are the simple-minded," and he said: "Because they were occupied with the bliss rather than the Bestower of it."

The majority of people read "fakihun" (فاكِهُونَ), meaning: possessors of fruit, as one says tamir (possessor of dates), laban (possessor of milk), shahim (possessor of fat) and lahim (possessor of meat). Abu Raja', Mujahid, Nafi' also, and Abu Ja'far read "fakihun" (فَكِهُونَ), meaning: joyful and merry, derived from fukaha (pleasantry), i.e., they have no worry. Talha, al-A'mash and a group read "fakihin" (فاكِهِينَ), making the predicate the adverbial phrase "fi shughl," with "fakihin" in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

His saying, exalted is He: "They and their spouses are in shade." "Hum" (هُمْ) is the subject, "wa azwajuhum" (وَأزْواجُهُمْ) is conjoined to it, and "fi zilal" (فِي ظِلالِ) is its predicate. It is possible that "hum" is a substitute for "fakihun," and "fi zilal" is then in the position of a circumstantial state, as if he said: "sheltering in shade." The majority read "fi zilal," the plural of "zill," since there is no sun in the Garden; its air is temperate, like the time of dawn before sunrise. It is possible that it is the plural of "zullah" (ظُلَّةٍ). Abu 'Ali said: like burmah and biram, and other examples. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: zilal is the plural of zillah with a kasra on the zad.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is a dialect form of zullah. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "fi zulal" (فِي ظُلَلٍ), which is the plural of zullah, and it is the reading of 'Abdullah, Talha and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. This expresses the coverings, levels and screens, such as canopies, curtains and the like, from things that provide shade and are adornment.

"Al-araik" (الأرائِكُ) are the furnished couches. Some people said: among its conditions is that it have a canopy over it; otherwise it is not an arika. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and 'Ikrima restricted it to this. Others said: the arika is a couch, whether or not it had a canopy.

His saying: "ma yad'un" (ما يَدَّعُونَ) is equivalent to "ma yatamannawn" (what they wish for). Abu 'Ubayda said: the Arabs say: "ud'i 'alayya ma shi'ta" (call upon me for whatever you wish), meaning: wish for me. They also say: "Fulan fima idda'a" (so-and-so is in what he claimed), meaning: in what he called for, since it is ifta'ala from da'a yad'u. The original form of this verb was yadtaʻiyun; the vowel of the ya' was moved to the ʻayn before it, the ya' was deleted because it coincided with the sakin waw, leaving yadtaʻun; the ta' was changed to dal and assimilated into the other, and the dal was specifically retained rather than the ta' because it is a letter of firmness (jald) while ta' is a letter of breathiness (hams). al-Rummani said: the meaning is that whoever claims something, it is his; because their characters have been refined, so they claim only what is becoming of them.

His saying: "Salam" (سَلامٌ). It was said: it is a description of "ma," meaning: it is granted to them and pure. It was said: it is a beginning (mubtada'), and it was said: it is the predicate of a beginning. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Ghanawi read "salaman" (سَلامًا) in the accusative as a verbal noun. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read "silm" (سِلْمٌ), which has the meaning of "salam." "Qawlan" (قَوْلًا) is in the accusative as a verbal noun.

His saying, exalted is He: "And stand apart today" – the verse. There is an omission in it; its estimate is: and He says to the disbelievers. This is a counterpart to His saying to the companions of the Garden: "Salam." "Imtazu" (امْتازُوا) means: separate yourselves and withdraw, because the people in the place of standing are only mixed together. Then He addressed them with what distinguishes them, as a reproach to them and a reminder of His charge to them and their violation of His charge. The majority read "a'had" (أعْهَدْ) with a fatha on the ha'. al-Hudhali and Ibn Wathhab read "alam i'had" (أَلَمِ إعْهَدْ) with a kasra on the mim and the hamza and a fatha on the ha', according to the dialect of those who vowel the initial letter of the imperfect with a kasra except the ya'. It is related from Ibn Wathhab "i'had" with a kasra on the ha'. It is said: 'ahida and 'ahada (both are used). "Ibadat al-Shaytan" (عِبادَةُ الشَيْطانِ) means: obeying him and submitting to his helpers. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "wa an u'budūni" (وَأنُ اعْبُدُونِي) with a damma on the nun of "an," following it with the damma of the ba' and dal and the waw of the plural as well. Talha, al-A'mash and a group read "fakihin" (فاكِهِينَ), making the predicate the adverbial phrase "fi shughl," with "fakihin" in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 62–65:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And he had already led astray a great multitude of you. Did you not then use reason?﴾ ﴿This is Hell which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Today We seal over their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾

This too is an address to the disbelievers, in the manner of rebuke.

And "al-jibil" (a multitude, a great nation): al-Naqqash related from al-Dahhak that the least of it is ten thousand, and there is no limit to its greater amount. Nafi' and 'Asim read it with a kasra on the jim and the ba' and a shadda on the lam, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Shayba, the people of Madina, Abu Raja', and al-Hasan (according to one report from him). Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read it with a kasra on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and without shadda. Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, and al-A'raj read it with a damma on the jim and the ba' and a shadda, and this is the reading of Abu Ishaq, 'Isa, and Ibn Thabit. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil read it with a damma on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and without shadda. Ibn Kathir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read [jubulan] with a damma on the jim and the ba' and without shadda. Abu Hatim reported from some Khurasanis a reading with a kasra on the jim and a silent ya' with two dots. The majority read ﴿takunu ta'qilun﴾ with the ta', and Talha read it with the ya'.

Then He placed them before Hell, which they were promised and used to deny. "Jahannam" is the first level of the Fire, and "isla-wha" means: enter it (lit. make direct contact with it).

Then the Blessed and Exalted informed Muhammad (ﷺ) of matters in which his community shares with him, by His saying: ﴿Today We seal over their mouths﴾, meaning: on that day this will happen. It is related in this sense that Allah causes the disbelievers to dispute, and when they bring nothing that establishes the proof, they revert to denial and deny the angels regarding the deeds. At that point Allah seals over their mouths, so they utter not a letter, and He commands their limbs to bear witness, so they testify. 'Uqba ibn 'Amir related from the Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, that he said: "Indeed the first part of the disbeliever to speak will be his left thigh." Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "The right one, then the rest of his limbs." It is also related that some of the disbelievers will say on that day to their limbs: "Ruin and destruction to you! **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 36, verses 71–76:**

His exalted and majestic words:

Will they not then be grateful?﴾ ﴿And they have taken, besides Allah, gods, that they might be helped.﴾ ﴿They are not able to help them, and they are for them an assembled host.﴾ ﴿So let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾

This is an address concerning the Quraysh, their turning away from the Sharia (sharʿ, divine law) and their worship of idols. In this verse Allah, exalted is He, draws their attention to His favour upon them through the beasts of the livestock.

His words "Our hands" (ʾaydīnā) are an expression for power. He expressed it with "yad" (hand), "yadayn" (two hands), and "aydin" (hands), because humans only understand power and seizing through the hand. So He spoke to them in terms of the aspect that is closest to their understanding, while Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is far above a limb and above all resemblance. His words, exalted is He, "so they are their owners" (fa-hum lahā mālikūn) are a reminder of the blessing, in that these livestock are not unruly or overpowering, but are kept and their benefits are brought near.

His words "We have made them subservient" (dhallalnāhā) mean: We made them subjugated and submissive. "Al-rakūb" (what is ridden) is the object ridden, and it is a form of *faʿūl* (faʿūl) with the meaning of *mafʿūl* (passive participle), and it occurs only in a limited set of words, such as *rakūb* (ridden), *ḥalūb* (milked), and *qadūʿ* (milk-yielding). The majority of readers recite *rakūbuhum* with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, while al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read it with a ḍammah. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) read *rakūbatuhum*. "Al-manāfiʿ" (benefits) refers to the wool, the fur, and other things, and "al-mashārib" (drinks) means the milk.

Then He rebuked them for taking gods in pursuit of help and support through them. Then He informed them that they are not able to do so. It is possible that the pronoun in *yastaṭīʿūna* refers to the disbelievers, and in *naṣrahum* to the idols; and it is possible that it is the reverse, because both meanings are correct.

His words, exalted is He, "and they are for them an assembled host" (wa-hum lahum jundun): it is possible that the first pronoun refers to the disbelievers and the second to the idols, meaning: these disbelievers are mobilised and banded together for these idols in this world, but despite that they are not able to support one another. It is also possible that it is the reverse, meaning: they will be brought before them in the Hereafter at the reckoning, in the sense of reproach and vengeance. In this interpretation He called them "host" because they are the instrument of vengeance upon them and of their reproach. The pronouns for the idols in this verse follow the pattern of those who have reason, since in their worship they were given the status of reason, so they were treated accordingly in the expression.

Then He comforted His Prophet (ﷺ) with His words: "So let not their speech grieve you," and He warned the disbelievers with His words: "Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 77–80:

(p-267) The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop of semen, and then he is an open adversary?﴾ ﴿And he sets forth for Us a comparison and forgets his own creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knowing of every creation."﴾ ﴿He who made for you from the green tree fire, and then from it you ignite.﴾

Ibn Jubayr said: These verses were revealed because "al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi came to the Prophet ﷺ with a decayed bone, crumbled it, and said: 'O Muhammad, who will give life to this?'" Mujahid and Qatadah said: The one who brought the rotten bone was Umayya ibn Khalaf. al-Hasan said the same, as mentioned by al-Rummani. Ibn 'Abbas radiya Allahu 'anhuma said: It was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an error on the part of the one who attributed it to Ibn 'Abbas, radiya Allahu 'anhuma, because the surah is Meccan, and the verse is Meccan by consensus, and because 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy never openly displayed such defiance. The name "Ubayy" is what became confused for the narrators, because the sound report is what Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, and what Ibn Ishaq and others said: "Indeed Ubayy ibn Khalaf, brother of Umayya ibn Khalaf, is the one who brought the decayed bone in Mecca and crumbled it in the face of the Prophet ﷺ, and said: 'Who will give life to this, O Muhammad?'" Ubayy had standings and statements with the Prophet ﷺ until he was killed by his hand at the Battle of Uhud with a spear, with a wound in his neck. It is narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him when he crumbled the bone: "Allah will give it life, and will give you life, and will cause you to enter Hell." Then the verse was revealed, establishing the proof that man is a drop of semen, and then after that becomes an open adversary. Is this not a bringing to life after death and non-existence?

His saying: ﴿And forgets﴾ may mean forgetfulness through heedlessness, and it may mean forgetfulness through abandonment. "al-Rameem" is that which is worn out and crumbled, and it is the dust.

(p-268) Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, directed them to reflect upon the first creation. Then He followed this with a third proof: the production of fire from the green wood that is full of water. This is the flint of the Arabs, and fire exists in every piece of wood, but it is more readily produced in the loose wood with open pores, such as al-Markh and al-'Afar. He returned the pronoun to "the tree" in the masculine, having regarded the wording, just as with "the dates," "the pebbles," and others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 81–83:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, indeed; He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿So glorified is He in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

This is an affirmation and a questioning about a matter whose soundness indicates the possibility of the resurrection of bodies from graves and the return of the dead.

The pronoun in His, the Glorified, saying ﴿"mithlahum" (their likes)﴾ is in the plural form used for those who have reason, because the two (the heavens and the earth) include those who have reason among the angels and the two weighty ones (humans and jinn). This is the interpretation of a group of the exegetes, while al-Rummani and others said: the pronoun refers to the people.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So they (the people) are an example of resurrection, and the verse is comparable to His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. Salam Abu al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ya'qub, and al-A'raj recited "wa-yaqdir" (and He is able) in the imperfect (al-istiqbal, the future/present tense), while the majority recited "bi-qadir" (able) in the active participle (ism al-fa'il, the active participle form). The majority recited "al-Khallaq" (the All-Creating), and al-Hasan recited "al-Khaliq" (the Creator).

He made "fayakunu" (and it is) in the nominative, on the meaning: "fa-huwa yakunu" (so it is), and this is the recitation of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kisa'i recited [fayakuna] in the accusative. Abu 'Ali said: al-Kisa'i does not put it in the accusative unless "an" (that) precedes it, while Ibn 'Amir put it in the accusative even if "an" does not precede it. The accusative here is the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin. His, the Exalted, saying ﴿"kun" (Be)﴾ is a command to the thing being brought into existence at the moment the power relates to it, not before that nor after it. It is commanded only as an emphasis on the power and as an indication of it. This is a command without letters or sounds, rather it is from His speech that subsists in His essence. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, declared Himself free of all imperfection with a general and absolute declaration of transcendence. The majority recited "malakut" (dominion), while al-A'mash and al-Taymi recited "malaka" (dominion/power), and its meaning is: the control of every thing and the power over it.

The commentary on Surah Ya-Sin is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

He made "fayakunu" (and it is) in the nominative, on the meaning: "fa-huwa yakunu" (so it is), and this is the recitation of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kisa'i recited [fayakuna] in the accusative. Abu 'Ali said: al-Kisa'i does not put it in the accusative unless "an" (that) precedes it, while Ibn 'Amir put it in the accusative even if "an" does not precede it. The accusative here is the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin. His, the Exalted, saying ﴿"kun" (Be)﴾ is a command to the thing being brought into existence at the moment the power relates to it, not before that nor after it. It is commanded only as an emphasis on the power and as an indication of it. This is a command without letters or sounds, rather it is from His speech that subsists in His essence. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, declared Himself free of all imperfection with a general and absolute declaration of transcendence. The majority recited "malakut" (dominion), while al-A'mash and al-Taymi recited "malaka" (dominion/power), and its meaning is: the control of every thing and the power over it.

The commentary on Surah Ya-Sin is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 36, verses 81–83:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, indeed; He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿So glorified is He in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

This is an affirmation and a questioning about a matter whose soundness indicates the possibility of the resurrection of bodies from graves and the return of the dead.

The pronoun in His, the Glorified, saying ﴿"mithlahum" (their likes)﴾ is in the plural form used for those who have reason, because the two (the heavens and the earth) include those who have reason among the angels and the two weighty ones (humans and jinn). This is the interpretation of a group of the exegetes, while al-Rummani and others said: the pronoun refers to the people.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So they (the people) are an example of resurrection, and the verse is comparable to His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people﴾ [Ghafir: 57].
